name: Dún

attributes.attribute: Celtic provincial capital by seventh century C.E.

sources: Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: Dún means fortress in Irish and Scottish Gaelic. The word names many mythological sites. Dún Ailinne was a great hillfort in County Kildare begun in Neolithic times. The Celts took it over as a provincial capital around the seventh century C.E. It now stands as Knockaulin Hill. Excavation has revealed large earthworks, a causeway, and foundations of ancient structures. The site bears the name of the obscure goddess Alend. Dún Aonghusa on the Aran Islands uses a sheer cliff for one side and stone walls for the rest. Legend says the Fir Bolg built it and named it after Angus, their chief. Dún Bolg was a battle site where Leinster warriors resisted the cow-tribute paid to the king of Tara. Dún Delgan, named for the Fomorian chief Delga, became the base of Cúchulainn.

okr.objective: Explain the meaning of dún and list the principal mythological sites that carry the name.
key_results: Dún means fortress in Irish and Scottish Gaelic.
Dún Ailinne was a hillfort in County Kildare and a Celtic provincial capital.
Legend credits the Fir Bolg with building Dún Aonghusa on the Aran Islands.
Dún Delgan, named for Delga, became the base of Cúchulainn.
evidence: Monaghan, Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore (2003): Dún.
